shower.thought: # Shower Thoughts
We measure our lives in time, but we only ever experience the present moment, so technically we're always living in an infinitely small fraction of our own existence.
You'll never know if you're remembering an event correctly or just remembering the last time you remembered it.
The people you envy are probably envying someone else, which means envy is just a game where everyone's looking backward instead of forward.
If you've ever changed your mind about something, you've proven that the person you were before doesn't actually exist anymore.
You're living in the only time period where you'll ever be alive, which makes it simultaneously the most important era and completely unremarkable.
The harder you work to be authentic, the less authentic it becomes, but the moment you stop trying is the moment you're finally genuine.
You can't miss something you never had, so happiness might just be forgetting about the alternate versions of your life that didn't happen.
Every embarrassing thing you did gets less funny to everyone else over time, but it stays exactly as mortifying to you forever.
We call it "falling in love" as if it's something that happens to you, not realizing you're falling toward someone who's falling toward you at the same time.
The only time you'll ever truly understand another person is when they stop trying to be understood.
You've probably had the most important conversation of your life without realizing it was happening.
The things you remember most vividly are often the ones that shaped you the least.
If everyone is a little bit broken, then wholeness might just be an illusion we invented to feel like we're aiming for something.
You're the protagonist of your own story and a background character in everyone else's, which is somehow both empowering and completely meaningless.
The older you get, the faster time moves, which means your subjective lifespan is actually shrinking even as your objective lifespan grows.
You trust your phone with more secrets than you trust most people, which means your phone knows you better than your friends do.
Boredom is just your brain telling you it's ready to grow, but we treat it like something to escape.
The version of yourself that exists in other people's minds will outlive the actual you.
You can't choose what makes you comfortable, which means you're partly a prisoner of your own preferences.

motivational.thought: The master has failed more times than the beginner has ever tried. — Stephen McCranie
Your future self is watching you right now through memories you haven't made yet. — Unknown
Comparison is the thief of progress. Focus on your own race. — Unknown
Small disciplines repeated with consistency every day lead to remarkable results over time. — James Clear
Everything worth doing is worth doing poorly at first. — Unknown
The difference between who you are and who you want to be is what you do. — Bill Phillips
You're not behind. You're not late. You're exactly where you need to be, learning what you need to learn. — Unknown
Success is not final, failure is not fatal: it is the courage to continue that counts. — Winston Churchill
The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek. — Joseph Campbell
Don't wait for permission to build the life you want. Start anyway. — Unknown
Progress over perfection, always. — Unknown
Your obstacles are not stopping you. Your mindset about them is. — Unknown
The person who says it cannot be done should not interrupt the person doing it. — Chinese Proverb
What lies behind you and what lies before you pales in comparison to what lies within you. — Ralph Waldo Emerson
One day you will wake up and there won't be time to do the things you always wanted to. Do it now. — Paulo Coelho
Motivation follows action, not the other way around. — Unknown
The cost of discipline is always less than the pain of regret. — Unknown
Your only limit is you. Everything else is just an excuse dressed up as a reason. — Unknown
We are not makers of history. We are made by history. — Martin Luther King Jr.
The struggle you're in today is developing the strength you need for tomorrow. — Robert Tew

darkjoke.thought:
My therapist asked me what my biggest fear is.
I said, "That one day you'll actually help me."

I told my friend he'd be great at networking.
He said, "Really?" I said, "Yeah, you're already good at making connections—mostly to people who never call you back."

My doctor said I need to cut back on sugar.
I said, "Doc, I'm already depressed enough."

I asked my dad if he believed in life after death.
He said, "I don't know, but based on your job prospects, you should."

My girlfriend said I'm emotionally unavailable.
I said, "That's not true." Then I didn't text her for three days to prove I cared.

I went to a self-help seminar about confronting your demons.
Turns out they just meant my issues, but I showed up ready for actual combat and felt really stupid.

My mom asked why I'm still single.
I said, "High standards." She said, "You date people who ghost you." I said, "Exactly—they have the decency to leave."

I asked my accountant if I'd ever be financially stable.
He laughed so hard he had to step out of the room. When he came back, he said, "Sorry, I needed that."

My friend said he's finally getting his life together.
I asked him for details. He said, "Well, I've accepted that it will never happen." That's actually progress for him.

I told my boss I wanted to discuss my future with the company.
He said, "Let's be real—your future with us is already behind you."

My therapist keeps telling me I need to live in the moment.
Which is ironic, because every moment I'm in is a disappointment.

I said to my date, "I'm not like other guys."
She said, "I know—they usually text back." I said, "That's what makes me special."

My friend asked if I thought he'd ever get married.
I said, "Only if you lower your standards significantly." He said, "I'm already dating you." I said, "Exactly my point."

I told my kid that Santa isn't real.
He said, "I know." I said, "Then who's been leaving presents?" He said, "You have, which is why they've been getting worse."

My doctor said I have the liver of a 60-year-old.
I said, "That's not possible—I'm 35." He said, "I know. It's aged remarkably fast."

I asked my friend how his new job was going.
He said, "It's killing me." I said, "That's called ambition." He said, "No, that's called a micromanager and untreated anxiety."

My ex said she needed space.
I gave her 2,000 miles and she still found a way to ruin my day.

I told my mom I was thinking about having kids.
She said, "Are you sure?" I said, "Why?" She said, "You still can't take care of yourself." I said, "That's a great point—never mind."

My dentist said I need to floss more.
I said, "You know what I really need?" He said, "What?" I said, "A better habit of avoiding things that give me anxiety."

I asked my friend if he believed in second chances.
He said, "After you stood me up last week? No." I said, "Good, because I'm definitely going to do it again."
